title: Does watching aggression lead to aggression?
claimTopic: whether watching aggression leads people to act more aggressively

sources.title: Source 1: Children after a violent or a calm cartoon

study.introduction: Researchers asked whether children act more aggressively in play right after watching a cartoon in which characters hit and kick each other.
study.participants: 80 children aged 6 to 9 from four elementary schools in Texas (42 girls and 38 boys) took part with a parent's written consent and their own assent. They were randomly assigned to two groups of 40.
study.method: One group watched a 15-minute cartoon with frequent hitting and kicking. The other watched a 15-minute cartoon with the same characters and no fighting. Each child then played for 10 minutes in a room with toys, including a foam punching bag. Two coders who did not know the child's group counted aggressive acts (hitting, kicking or throwing a toy, or pushing the bag over).
study.results: Children who watched the violent cartoon made a mean of 5.2 aggressive acts in 10 minutes. Children who watched the calm cartoon made a mean of 2.4. The difference was statistically significant.
study.discussion: The children copied many of the specific moves the cartoon characters used.

plot.label: Bar graph of mean aggressive acts in 10 minutes of play: 5.2 after a violent cartoon and 2.4 after a calm cartoon (invented data)

sources.title: Source 2: Violent games at 13 and aggression at 15

study.introduction: Researchers asked whether teens who play more violent video games become more aggressive over the following two years.
study.participants: 412 teens (ages 13 at the start; 51% girls) from public schools in three Midwestern cities and their parents took part with consent and assent.
study.method: At age 13, teens reported how many hours a week they played games rated for violence, and were grouped as low (0 to 2 hours), medium (3 to 7) or high (8 or more). At ages 13 and 15, teachers rated each teen's physical aggression at school on a scale from 1 (never) to 5 (very often).
study.results: At 15, mean teacher ratings were 2.1 for the low group, 2.3 for the medium group and 2.6 for the high group. Hours of violent gaming correlated with aggression at 15 at r = .12. When the researchers took into account aggression at 13 and family conflict, the link fell to r = .04.
study.discussion: The researchers concluded that violent gaming predicted later aggression only weakly, and that much of the link could be explained by other factors.

plot.label: Bar graph of mean teacher-rated aggression at age 15 by violent gaming at 13: low 2.1, medium 2.3, high 2.6 on a 1 to 5 scale (invented data)

sources.title: Source 3: How long does the effect last?

study.introduction: Researchers asked whether a short violent film clip raises aggression in young adults, and whether any effect lasts 30 minutes.
study.participants: 120 college students (ages 18 to 22) at a university in California volunteered for course credit, gave informed consent and were debriefed afterward.
study.method: Students were randomly assigned to watch a 10-minute violent film clip or a 10-minute nonviolent clip, and to be tested either right away or after a 30-minute filler task. In the test, students set the loudness of a noise blast for a supposed partner in a reaction-time game, from 1 (soft) to 10 (very loud). No noise was ever actually played to anyone.
study.results: Tested right away, students who saw the violent clip chose a mean loudness of 5.8, compared with 4.6 after the nonviolent clip. After 30 minutes, the means were 4.9 and 4.7, a difference too small to be distinguished from chance.
study.discussion: Violent images may make aggressive thoughts easier to reach for a short time.

plot.label: Grouped bar graph of mean noise loudness chosen, right away and after 30 minutes: violent clip 5.8 and 4.9, nonviolent clip 4.6 and 4.7 (invented data)

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based on at least one of the provided sources that responds to the question: Does watching aggression lead to aggression?

rubric.point: States a defensible claim that answers whether watching aggression leads to aggression
accept: Watching aggression leads to more aggression in the short term, especially in children who copy what they see
Watching aggression raises aggression briefly, but the long-term effect is weak
Watching aggression has only a small effect on later aggression

parts.sample: Watching aggression makes people, especially children, act more aggressively right afterward, but the effect is small and short-lived over the long term.

parts.label: B(i)
parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.

rubric.point: Gives a specific, accurate result from one source and cites the source
accept: According to Source 1, children who watched the violent cartoon made a mean of 5.2 aggressive acts compared with 2.4 after the calm cartoon
In Source 3, students chose louder noise blasts (5.8) right after a violent clip than after a nonviolent clip (4.6)

parts.sample: According to Source 1, children who watched a violent cartoon made a mean of 5.2 aggressive acts in 10 minutes of play, more than twice the 2.4 acts of children who watched a calm cartoon.

parts.label: B(ii)
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding learned in AP® Psychology.

rubric.point: Explains how the evidence supports the claim
accept: The children who saw violence acted more aggressively right after watching, which fits a short-term effect

rubric.point: Applies a psychology concept (not a restricted term) to the evidence and links it to the claim

parts.sample: This supports my claim because the children acted aggressively right after watching, and they copied the characters' specific moves. This is modeling: children attend to a model, remember what it did and imitate it. The cartoon characters were models who hit and kicked without any punishment, so the children reproduced those acts in play, which shows watching aggression led to more aggression soon after.

parts.label: C(i)
parts.prompt: Support your claim using a different piece of specific and relevant evidence from another source.

rubric.point: Gives a specific, accurate result from a different source and cites it
accept: In Source 3, the violent-clip group chose 5.8 versus 4.6 right away, but 4.9 versus 4.7 after 30 minutes
Source 2 found that violent gaming at 13 correlated only r = .12 with aggression at 15, and r = .04 once earlier aggression and family conflict were taken into account

parts.sample: Source 3 found that students who watched a violent clip chose louder noise blasts right away (5.8 versus 4.6), but after 30 minutes the two groups were almost the same (4.9 versus 4.7).

parts.label: C(ii)
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding learned in AP® Psychology.

rubric.point: Explains how the evidence supports the claim
accept: The effect appeared right away and was gone after 30 minutes, so it is short-lived

rubric.point: Applies a different psychology concept from B(ii) (not a restricted term) and links it to the claim

parts.sample: This supports the short-lived part of my claim because of priming. The violent clip activated aggressive ideas, which made aggressive responses easier to reach for a short time, so students set louder blasts right away. Priming fades, which explains why the difference had almost disappeared 30 minutes later.
